utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yours is not -- so let's report that straight away. May I draw the attention of the technician or technicians that the microphone of Ms. Korner is not working. Actually, it seems that -- no one is switched on now, the one to your right --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's some -- it is working to speak. The interpretation channels are not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. And you are on number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Nothing happens when you go either up or down. It's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you checked the volume?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what it's not doing is showing any sort of a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could one of the technicians please come to the courtroom, please, and check this out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may well be it's just me being incompetent. Sorry, I'll say it again. Because the headphones weren't plugged in either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't tell me that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Even I have to admit to incompetence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That completes the Trial Chamber, as it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you call the case, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you too. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Talic. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, having recovered from my technical incompetence, it's Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman with legal assistant Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. And appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. My name is Maitre de Roux, and I'm assisted by Madam Fauveau-Ivanovic for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. I see that General Talic is happier than the last few days, having you here in the courtroom. Welcome. Now, Ms. Korner, we do have some preliminaries. And I see that along the line of -- lines of the incompetence that you referred to earlier, we have brought the witness in the courtroom when I know that you have some preliminary issues to address.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not incompetence. I was asked about this, and it seemed to me it would be better if the witness could finish his evidence and then we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is all right with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is. There's only one very quick matter that I need to raise because steps have to be carried out. Your Honour will recall that at the request of Mr. Ackerman, you issued an order that the witness who had the many files which contained letters, should produce them. The -- what has happened is the whole file has been sent up from Sarajevo. What did we intend to do -- and I'm raising it, so that's there's any objection. It seems to me that the whole file will be confidential. We're going to go through it, in the sense of extract the letters that Mr. Ackerman asked for, if there are any; photocopy them, and make those the exhibits, if necessary. In other words, keep those in our possession. And return the whole original files to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That -- Mr. Ackerman, I don't think I need to consult you or Maitre de Roux on this matter, because it's something which is obvious. That's the best way how to handle the file. And the Chamber leaves it entirely in your responsibility to do exactly what you have just suggested. In actual fact, I think you should also restrict yourself to the bear minimum of these documents. If they are repeated -- in other words, if they -- if that gentleman had so many visitors, not to use the proper word, who all gave him the same kind of documents, I think if we have half a dozen of them, that should -- that should be enough. We don't need the entire lot. We don't need to know exactly how many of such visitors did he have or he worked for, you know ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Ackerman is happy with that -- if there are a load of these letters saying they have been dismissed as a result of the Crisis Staff decisions, we will simply extract half a dozen or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that be okay with you, Mr. Ackerman, or do you want them all here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we're going to have to deal with a load. I'd be surprised if there's even one. But we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll see. If there are a load, then I agree. Six is probably enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, so that's the position. I mean, use your discretion, Ms. Korner. No one is going to tell you why did you bring only six when there was 100? I mean, if there is 100, use your discretion. If there are seven, I mean, it would be a very silly discretion if you don't bring the seven of them and you only bring six. I mean -- so it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that indication and to Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So now I understand we can proceed with the witness. And then you will make the submissions later on. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Speaking of incompetence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I apologise for mine at the close of yesterday's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. I mean, I realised that everyone was tired at that point in time, and I was trying to restrain myself because the bundle that I had did not correspond to the order that you were presenting them, in any case. So -- but I was trying to do my best to cope at that point in time. But at a certain moment, it became impossible. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no -- Ms. Sutherland, you don't need to say any more. Just let's get along with the exercise that we have to do. And just to help you, just tell us now from which point number Exhibit 537 starts and finishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 537 -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 537.1 is a record of interview with the accused Zeljko Ceko compiled on the 10th of December 1992 before the investigating judge, Slavko Stupar, of the military court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can simplify it even further. What I suggest you do is: First you tell us how many documents you're tendering under 4. -- under disclosure number 4.1255, how many documents you're going to tender.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, in total there's 13 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 13 documents. So now what I would suggest to do is you go through them one by one, starting with 537.1, telling us how many pages and starting from which page -- translation page to which page, so that you don't have to explain exactly what the document is about or the date or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. I have actually -- and I should -- and this is what I should have done yesterday was pre-marked the exhibit numbers which happened last night. The documents have been recopied, and those copies have been provided to Your Honour and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So document 5. -- sorry, 537.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is translation number 03050443.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Through?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct. So that becomes number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Exhibit 537.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is translation number 03046313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Ackerman and Maitre de Roux, are you following --

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I tried to simplify it as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have them. They're all marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But I just want to make sure -- the duty of the Chamber is to make sure that marking corresponds to what Ms. Sutherland is stating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no doubt that it does. As far as I'm concerned, we don't need to go through this exercise, but if the Court wishes, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're happy with what you have, we can just put the stickers on them and we can proceed and you just tender the whole bundle and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise for the confusion it created yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem, Ms. Sutherland. These things happen. So you don't have to apologise at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that -- did you have 538 and 539 and 540 have already been tendered. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So I understand you don't have any further questions to the witness, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And have the Defence teams agreed who's going to start first? Maitre de Roux?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Fauveau, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just at the start of the cross-examination, could I -- could we go into private session, because I have some details to ask that require private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were talking about mosques, and you said that they were later destroyed. Would you agree with the statement that all those mosques that were destroyed were destroyed in 1993? And I'm talking about the mosques in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday during my testimony, I said clearly that all religious facilities, mosques, shops, houses that belonged to non-Serb population were constantly exposed to shooting. The fact that it is testified by many traces, and this wasn't just in 1993. In 1993 after all the mosques were destroyed, this was already a fait accompli. But the actual destruction of the mosques started much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether -- were the mosques destroyed in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer, sir. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript says the answer to the last question that the witness said "the fact that it is testified many traces and this wasn't just in 1993." That makes no sense to me. Maybe it's just that I don't understand the English language as well as I thought I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My transcript says exactly the same thing. Probably it could have been -- I don't know, testimony or ... Is it possible to go back -- to play back that part in the original -- in the French --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understand the B/C/S, and I believe that corresponds exactly to what the witness said. But in any case, it does not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Were the mosques destroyed in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mosques were destroyed completely to the ground in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke of the meetings that you had with the Banja Luka mayor, Mr. Radic. And you said that these meetings began in the period which followed the mobilisation in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with that that a lot of Muslims did not respond to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 there was war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But Croatia at the time was seeking independence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, Bosnia was still a part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday when I was asked about the situation in Banja Luka in 1991 and 1992, I said that the situation was unbearable, that it was very difficult and very hard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The question was: Was Bosnia independent or was it still part of Yugoslavia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know that it was part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday during these meetings with Mr. Radic, Mr. Radic was promising to take steps but that he never did anything. On page 4 of your written testimony -- written statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could I ask the Prosecutor to give the statement to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 4 of your statement, you spoke of these meetings with Mr. Radic, and you said that after these meetings the Serb police started to patrol the Muslim neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the patrolling improved the situation? On the contrary; the patrols made the situation a lot worse. The patrols were mistreating the people. And I have thousands of pieces of evidence for that if you need that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were talking about the abbreviation SOS, and you said that these abbreviations stood for the Serbian defence forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at your written statement. You were also speaking about the SOS in your statement, and you said that this stood for the Serb liberation forces. Which one of these two statements is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I believe that it's "Serb defence forces," because the Serbs always said that they were attacked and that they needed to defend themselves. But whether it's "defence" or "liberation forces," I think that's a side issue. This is -- these are people who brought a lot of evil to Banja Luka and who then later became blackmailers and -- asking for extra tax. So I don't think that it's actually very important whether they were defence forces or liberation forces. The abbreviation was SOS, and we know what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were talking about the checkpoints in Banja Luka. And you said that in the summer of 1992, there were checkpoints in Banja Luka. Could you tell us when the checkpoints were established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The checkpoints were established immediately at the beginning. It was in spring, in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise and give us the month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was April. I think that it was April.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the referendum on the independence of Bosnia took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please address such questions to politicians. I'm a businessman. And I was not interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But during the referendum, were you in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the two days of the referendum, were there any barricades in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me now when that referendum took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to give you the same answer I gave you a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait. Wait. Wait. I was very patient when you replied to the question put to you by the Defence counsel for General Talic the way you did. You have to behave in this courtroom the same way that everybody else is behaving with you. The Defence team for General Talic and the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin have every right to put questions to you. And if they are legitimate questions, if they are questions that are allowed by the Trial Chamber because they are according to the Rules of this Court, then you are in duty bound to answer them. Now, I was tolerant. You were not right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to answer that question or to answer the way that you did, setting the dates -- fixing the dates of a referendum or an election is the business of a political party. But the dates when that referendum or the dates when that general election was held is another matter. That is something which is of public consumption and that is something which the general public either knows or doesn't know. But you as a member of the community of Banja Luka, I suppose you are in a position to answer it by saying, "Yes, I remember the dates. These are the dates," or "I'm sorry. I don't remember the dates." If you really don't remember the dates. You have no right to treat Defence counsel the way that you did, and you will be stopped if you do it again and brought to order. So now please, Madam Fauveau, I ask you to repeat the question. And may I ask the witness to answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for drawing my attention to this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday of murder that took place in Banja Luka on the 5th of December, 1992. And the victims were Ramiz Zdenac, and Avdo Softic is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Softic, yes, and Ramiz Zdenac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The place where the murder took place was a place that was not frequented by Serbs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the place where the murder took place is a neighbourhood of Banja Luka inhabited by Muslims, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And at the time of the murder, it was already night-time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many people were there in the street at the time of the murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number of people, but I said, and I stand by what I said, that there were quite a number of people in groups of twos and threes. I don't think more than three persons to a group, because we were not allowed to gather in larger groups. And that was the only place where we thought in those days that we were safe. We felt safer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And just then, in that street, was Ceko the only Serb there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that Ceko fired because he was afraid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's out of the question. I said yesterday that all our people had been instructed and advised. I personally advised them and asked them not to engage in any conversation or any discussions, passing on the experiences of Mr. Radic, who said that a nasty look would be sufficient to provoke a Serb soldier to use his weapon. And especially, I told them, with respect to Softic and Zdenac, these were very, very quiet, warm, fine men, so there's no theoretic possibility even that they could have provoked a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that was not my question. I didn't say that they provoked Ceko. My question was simply whether he may have been afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what he could have been afraid of.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you were present when this murder took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every Serb in Banja Luka knew that Muslims, if any, the few that were there, were certainly unarmed. Earlier on this was a child who grew up amongst us, and there were never any problems until that fatal night. I don't know why he could have been scared and what he could have been scared of. Would any one of us scared walkers have had the strength to insult or provoke an armed Serb soldier? I beg you to tell me, is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present when this murder took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you saw Zeljko Ceko walking up to you. How was he going towards you? Was he in a car? Was he on foot? On a bicycle? How was he approaching you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said this yesterday. He was guiding his bicycle and walking along it, and he carried sidearms. And I'm not sure now. I know it was a long-barreled weapon. Now, whether it was a rifle or a light machine-gun, because they were almost the same. There was very little difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you on the scene of the crime when the police arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was the civilian police or the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For us, they were all the same. They wore the same uniforms. They performed the same duties. Now, whether they were called civilian or military, believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't make any distinction between the military police and the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were saying yesterday, we were talking about the military police with the white belts. These were -- did not have those belts. They were wearing blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Ceko was arrested after this murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I said yesterday loud and clear. And I will repeat what I said now. He was taken into custody, interrogated, because I would see him in the street. He was not in prison. And his punishment was to be sent to the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any proceedings against him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you personally were not called to testify as a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday, and I'll repeat. No one, not even the closest relatives of the victims, were called to testify, let alone me or the 10 or 15 of us that were there. I don't know now for sure, in view of the fear and the crowd. But no one was ever called to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness document P537. That is the indictment. [In English] The document 537.8.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you have before you indictment against Zeljko Ceko, dated the 8th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see the date of the 10th of May, 1993, but I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the 10th of May on the stamp, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph, beginning --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. The 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is the second page in English. The first paragraph on page 2 of the English version and in Serbo-Croatian it is second paragraph on the first page, beginning with the words: [In English] "For the following reasons, 19 hours on 5 December 1992 in Banja Luka." [Interpretation] Is that the description of the murder that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, Zeljko did not commit anything else, so judging by the names I see that this is the case that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now look at the second page, please, or page 4 in the English version, the paragraph beginning with the words [In English] "The following persons were heard as witnesses during the investigation." [Interpretation] Have you found that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the name Ajsa Dedusic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And a bit further down Bahrudin Spahic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And a little further on Dakir Imamovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then a in the next paragraph Suad Krnalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Suada Krnalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph Sakib Coco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are these people Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were those persons present at the scene of the crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were, as were many others.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've finished with that document, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a problem with the computer monitor. We can't see anything that's being put on the ELMO. I don't know why, but it's not coming through on the computer monitor channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you pressed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've pressed every button. Everything is plugged in. I'm not about to join --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put just one document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Your Honour. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you put any document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's there now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This sitting is jinxed, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as long as you have raised the issue, I'm a big fan of capitalism; but I think the OTP trying to sell coffee cups by putting ads on the backs of documents they give us is a little over the top. And maybe they tried to sell them to you too. If you look on your exhibits, you might find an ad on the back of the pages for a coffee cup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may be on yours, but not ours, Mr. Ackerman. Let's go on. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've come to my last group of questions. Yesterday you said that in 1992 a policeman came to see you and to seize your cars from you. I'm not talking about the Mercedes but the other vehicles you had. I'm talking about the incident when the two policemen came to your house and took you to the police station after that. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. I said two inspectors. That is how the other people addressed them. They were in civilian clothes, and they had pistols on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, sir. You said that this was in the summer of 1992. Could you possibly be more precise and tell us the month?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Madam Fauveau, I have a strong impression that the -- Ms. Sutherland for the Prosecution insisted on that same question twice yesterday, and it was still the reply -- the answer of the witness that he couldn't remember with precision except that he could confirm to us that it was certainly summer. But he couldn't say whether it was July, August, or whatever. I will allow the question again. And if the witness can be more precise, perhaps he could tell us. Otherwise, we could go on. Yes, sir. Do you remember more precisely the month or the week or the date, the precise date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have said it immediately yesterday. I only know that it was quite warm, and I don't know the exact month.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And at the time, one of your cars, the Mercedes, had already been taken; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I'm asking you once again for precision. It's very important for my case. Could you tell us roughly how much time prior to the arrival of these two policemen was your Mercedes seized? If you don't know, tell me that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, but Mr. Samardzija said that he already knew that the Mercedes had been seized. But I don't know exactly when that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau is right. Perhaps you could tell us whether it was a question of days before, whether it was a question of weeks before, or whether it was a question of months before that the Mercedes was taken from you until you were taken or asked to go to the police station.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, it wasn't long after that. Maybe a month or two on the outside. But I don't dare claim with a hundred percent degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness Exhibit P540. And please do not put it on the ELMO, as it contains confidential information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the certificate you spoke of yesterday and which, according to you, testifies to the fact that your vehicle was seized? The receipt, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You find the letters "MZ" on the right-hand side of that document. Did you see those letters? Don't those letters stand for local commune, or Mjesna Zajednica? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at the bottom right-hand corner of that document. That is your signature, is it not? Could you read --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read the words printed above. Could you read those words, please, just above your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Summons received."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now look at the signature on the left-hand side of that document and read the words printed just above that signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Summons delivered by."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at that receipt very closely, please. Do you agree with me that that receipt doesn't testify to the fact that your vehicle was taken but only that you received a summons to deliver the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can't agree, because I read the solemn declaration yesterday that I would speak the truth and nothing but the truth. And now if I say that this is a summons means that I was lying. This is a document that I received when I handed over my vehicle and the content. Surely you will not blame me for it. Now, whether this is a summons -- if it says "a summons delivered by such and such a person," one of the three who came -- I don't even know who signed it -- I would be able to recognise the person if I saw him now. I don't know his first or last name. I had to be the other party to say that I had received the summons. But I claim that this is the document that was given to me when I handed over my vehicle. And it's easy to check whether I was the owner of the vehicle, whether the vehicle was confiscated, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clarify this, because I think it's important for the Chamber to know as well. Looking at this document again, sir, what's the first word, the first line right in the middle, Potvrda? Can you read that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Potvrda, receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then the next line, Sopstvenik, that means your name. No? Without the need to pronounce it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Owner. It means owner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sopstvenik, means owner, okay. And the next line potvrdujemo prijem poziva, can you read that, please, the whole line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I confirm receipt of the summons for the execution of a material obligation for the OSDARU --" shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "M/V Mercedes 200 D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke of a person called Crnobrnja. Do you remember that? Do you remember that person? Is Crnobrnja a name that exists in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, you've asked me several questions and I'll answer in order. I do remember I spoke about Mr. Milo Crnobrnja, a member of the 4th Light Infantry Brigade headquartered in the Deumic's factory. As far as I know in Deumic's factory, Crnobrnja, as far as I know is not a Serb surname from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether Crnobrnja was a surname that exists in Bosnia, not in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia, probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that you spoke yesterday about Crnobrnja, who was in the 4th Light Infantry Brigade. But yesterday you said -- and that is on page 56: [In English] "Before that I, met this policeman whose name was Crnobrnja." [Interpretation] Are you sure that these two persons are one in the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Milorad Crnobrnja had a direct contact with me. He's not from Banja Luka. By occupation, he's a waiter. He's tall -- well, roughly about 170, 175 centimetres, well built, probably in his 30s. Again, don't hold me to my word. Maybe a year more or less. You may tell me tomorrow that I said he was 30, and he was 28. So he was about 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're telling us now that the name of this person is Milorad Crnobrnja. But yesterday during your testimony you did not know his first name. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Crnobrnja. I told you from the beginning, because he came several times. We had several contacts. And I know exactly the person I'm talking about. If you want me to be even more precise, he came with Mr. Jovo Sovilj when there was a report that the bridge at Novoselija had been mined. And Mr. Jovo, whom I considered to be a good man, said to him that I was a person that he could trust in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was that yesterday during your testimony here in court you did not know his first name. You saw his first name on a document; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I know who the man is, sometimes -- believe me -- I forget even people closest to me. But I can claim with a hundred percent certainty that I'm referring to the person from the 4th Light Infantry Brigade, because nobody called him by his first name Milorad but by Crnobrnja. As you know, it's very frequent in our part of the world for people to be addressed by their surnames.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you answer very briefly. His first name, you did not know it. You saw it on the documents provided by the Prosecutor; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps at one moment I had a kind of blockade and I couldn't remember. But it was not a different man. I stand by what I said. This is the same man. This is the man in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, yesterday on page 56 of the transcript, you said: "[In English] I don't know exactly his first name."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could say that about Stevandic as well, because I knew Stevandic personally, their commander. And I also said about the young man Zeljko Ceko in the first statement that his name was Dragan. Believe me, these are -- this is a question of years and time passing. Sometimes people forget. But we cannot forget what they are and who they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to something different, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more further questions. I'll make you very happy, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Ackerman. Now, Mr. Ackerman, as I explained to you yesterday, is the lead counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin. He has every right to put questions to you, and your duty is to answer the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you still have before you the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You -- when you began your testimony in this case, I believe you pointed out some errors that you had found in that statement and corrected them here in open court. One of them had to do with a statement that said only the Mercedes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes that. Only the Mercedes was in your name. And you changed that to all the vehicles were in your name. And the other change had to do with a statement that the Serbs asked if they could come in your house. And you then said that wasn't the case; that they didn't ask, they just came in. Those are the two changes that I recall. It's not important that I recall them all. But I have some questions I want to ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have also the English version of your statement there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Just the one in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask that the English version be provided to you, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, the Prosecutor has the English version over there, if you want to go and get it and bring it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first thing, sir: It's the case, is it not, that this statement was taken in the course of an interview on 3 October 2001? Last October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the English version of the statement, you will see some handwriting on the bottom of each page. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean these signs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It looks like signatures or initials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the marks there, would that be your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My signature is above what looks like to be initials. My signature is visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it appears on each page, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber how it was you came to sign each one of these pages. How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was giving the statement, which lasted several hours, there was the investigator and the interpreter. And after the end of the interview and the giving of the statement, I signed each of these pages and this is the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you read English, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand a little, but I don't speak it. I can understand a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So did you then read each one of these pages in English and confirm that it was what you said, or did someone read it to you, or how did it -- your signature there at the bottom is, as I understand it, your confirmation of the accuracy of the material on that page. How did you know what the page said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statement was of course read back to me, and they asked me if there was anything that I wanted to change or add. And after I answered that I did not, there followed the signing of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was read to you in your language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it your contention then, that the translator that was reading it to you did not read it to you accurately with regard to these two changes that you made yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that because of the vehicles, I was given a beating and Mr. Samardzija told me, "You're lying," because he knew that the vehicles were in my name, they were registered in my name. And that's the true. But how the actual error happened, a mistake happened, that was the translator's error, I don't know. But I noticed it after I was given it to have a look at both mistakes. It was not my mistake. And it's true what I'm saying. All vehicles were registered in my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so it's your position that is -- the changes you made actually reflect what you told the investigator during this interview in October of last year. You didn't tell the investigator the things that appear in this statement that you say are incorrect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that all the vehicles were in my name and that my associates were using the vehicles. That is what I wanted to say in my statement. This is what I am stating here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's what you also told the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor in October; is that your position that you told them the same thing that you've told us with regard to these two matters that you've changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I am standing by. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I'm trying to clear up. In the -- in the first -- it's the first page of your statement. The English version is actually page 2. It has a paragraph. The last paragraph begins with the words: "The leaders of the SDA in Banja Luka ...." Can you find that in the B/C/S version, "The leaders of the SDA in Banja Luka." I think it's on page 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you said in your statement is: "The leaders of the SDA in Banja Luka --" I'm sorry. That's not the paragraph I want to refer you to. It's my mistake. I want to refer you to the next paragraph, beginning: "The leaders of the SDS party in Banja Luka ...."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say that The leaders of the SDS party in Banja Luka were Radovan Vukic, Radoslav Brdjanin, Nikola Koljevic, and Ostoja Kremenovic. Was Nikola Koljevic from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was Ostoja Kremenovic from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What evidence do you have, sir, other than what you may have heard from someone, that Mr. Brdjanin was a leader of the SDS party in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said was that as far as politics were concerned -- I'd ask you to spare me. What I said here, I stand by what I said. The exact posts, the number of people, what their duties were, this kind of question just wouldn't suit me. But I know for certain that Radovan Vukic was the president of the SDS in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the question may not suit you, but I would like an answer. Do you have any evidence, other than what someone told you, that Mr. Brdjanin was a leader of the SDS party in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can be very specific, actually, sir. You can say, if that is the case, everyone knew it, it was always in the papers. When he was appointed president, it was announced in the paper, on TV, on the radio. It's got nothing to do with politics or involvement in politics. I know who the all the ministers and undersecretaries in the government of my country are, not because I have gone to the archives. I can go back to the beginning of the century and tell -- give you the whole list one by one, not because I am involved in politics or I like politics but because I -- I just know. If you ask me, I have read about them. So go ahead. Answer the question. In your statement, you didn't say, "I know that they were members of the SDS party. I presume that they were members of the SDS party." You said that they were leaders of the SDS party. So you had no problems with stating that they were leaders. And now you just have to answer how did you come to know that they were the leaders of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. Yes, that's what I'm claiming now, because the media were available. And you know that. Each one of us was able to see it, to hear it, and to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it is your position that in the media in Banja Luka it was reported that Mr. Brdjanin was a leader of the Banja Luka SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said one of the leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's what I said too, "one of the leaders." And I have to ask you the question again. It is your position, sir, that in the media in Banja Luka Mr. Brdjanin was reported to be a leader, one of the leaders, of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, can you be more specific? Was it the radio or the television or the newspaper or all three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So if we look at every issue of Glas for that period of time, we will find that story; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, that's not a fair question to come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll drop it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want you to go down -- you don't actually have to look at this unless you wish. It's about two paragraphs down. It begins with: "In 1991." You're talking about businesses of non-Serbs being blown up in late 1991 and into 1992. Isn't it the case that about 20 per cent of the businesses that were blown up were Serb businesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot speak about the percentages, but I know for sure, as I put in the statement, the roasting -- coffee roasting facility owned by Muslims was blown up. A grocery store was also blown up. That's what I stated, and that's what I'm stating now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what you stated was that the explosions were in businesses owned by non-Serbs. And all I'm asking you is: Wasn't it the case that there were also explosions in businesses owned by Serbs? In fact, about 20 per cent of them were in businesses owned by Serbs. Now, you can either tell me that you know that or you don't know it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's take it one by one, Mr. Ackerman, because you've mixed the two together. And in the question you're also suggesting that there were 20 per cent. So let's leave that for the time being and put the first question. Are you aware or do you know whether in 1991 and 1992 businesses of Serbs were also blown up and not only those of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about the Serb businesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the second question, therefore, now, doesn't fit in any more, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, sir, about attending a rally in Banja Luka of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any rallies of the SDA in Banja Luka or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that the theme of SDA rallies was to try to get people to become part of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday, if you remember, sir, that all the parties in the electoral campaign offered such programmes and were promising rose gardens in Bosnia. And I think that you remember that as well. And it is normal that in such promotional rallies, each party wanted to have as many voters as possible, which is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every party wants as many members in their ranks as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you attend any rallies of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not so much the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you attend even one HDZ rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not directly at a rally, but I spoke to their leading people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were also other parties active in Banja Luka at this -- at this time during this run-up to the elections, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those that were most active, as far as I'm concerned, were the nationalist parties: The SDS, the SDA, the HDZ. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't even know a name of the -- one of the parties at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you followed what I said correctly, then I said I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a socialist party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You claimed in your testimony that you saw Mr. Brdjanin often on TV at the end of 1991, the beginning of 1992. What television station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first I saw Mr. Brdjanin on Bosnian TV, because this is what I think was true. I believe that he was a deputy, that he was a Serb representative in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you saw him on television coming out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What other TV did you see him on? What other station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later we saw him on the Serb TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Coming from where? From Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the centre was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you heard Mr. Brdjanin in one of his -- or more -- one or more of his speeches advocate the destruction, the destroying of persons in mixed marriages. You told us that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you stand by that statement today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that it was not Mr. Brdjanin who said that but Dr. Vukic. Isn't that the case that it was Dr. Vukic you heard say that, not Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am certain -- I believe that this was said by Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that inasmuch as Mr. Brdjanin's two brothers are both in mixed marriages that he would have neither thought or uttered such words?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. The form of that question is objectionable. Whether these are mixed marriages or not is pure comment. He's made the suggestion, very properly, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm putting my case to him. She wants me to do it. Now she's objecting to me doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But you could put your case in a rephrased manner, Mr. Ackerman. You could first ask him whether he knows the facts that you are suggesting and whether -- and then you -- I am not going to tell you or suggest to you the way you should put the question to the witness. But Ms. Korner is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that Mr. Brdjanin has two brothers that at the time and today are in mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's the case, isn't it, that you did not hear Mr. Brdjanin make such a statement? That if you heard someone make it, it was Dr. Vukic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already answered that question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You claim, sir, to have seen SOS soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- for the first time in the summer of 1991 at the municipal building; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I think so, and that's what I think now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you are not certain about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about them much before. But as far as I remember, the first time I saw them was in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there's no question in your mind that you heard of the SOS and even saw SOS in the year 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And are you as certain about that as you are about all the other things you've told us in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Don't put a question to me linked to time, back of events took place ten years ago, and do not place it on equal footing with judgement of my entire statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what you're telling me in that answer, I guess, is that you're not really certain about when you first heard of or saw SOS soldiers, and you're just guessing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I need to repeat for a third time, I said "I think."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, you said -- the question was: "There's no question in your mind that you heard of the SOS and even saw SOS in the year 1991; right?" And your answer was: "I have no doubts." Now, that's different from "I think," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Ackerman, before -- let's read the whole sequence. "You claim, sir, to have seen the SOS soldiers?" "Yes." "For the first time in the summer of 1991 at the municipal building; correct?" "Yes." "Do you stand by that statement?" "I said I think so, and that's what I think now." "So you are not certain about that." "I heard about them much before. But as far as I remember, the first time I saw them was in the summer of 1991." "So there's no question in your mind that you heard of the SOS and even saw SOS in the year 1991; right?" "I have no doubt." I don't -- I don't think you are entitled to ask for more than you have been told already, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, when he says "I have no doubt," that's different from his saying "I think that I saw them in 1991."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, he has no doubt as to what you stated before. Because you are trying to extract from him a different statement. He was just confirming or reconfirming his previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think that's what it says, so I'll ask him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it the case that you saw SOS soldiers or heard of them in 1991? And if that's the case, are you certain about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I think that I had heard about them in the summer of 1991 and saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'll leave it at that. You gave us yesterday the names of several persons who you personally know were picked up by this red van you talked about. You remember giving us those names yesterday, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that happened? When were those people picked up by that red van? And I know you're not going to be able to give me an exact date, but get as close as you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My statement yesterday is the same as what I'm saying now. From the beginning of the arrest and persecution of non-Serbs, it was not just the red van that was operating. I said there was a white one and a blue one and a red one; therefore, at different times, at different periods. And I never said that those men were picked up altogether but at different times. But mostly by the red van and in various places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we talking of 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1992. The first half of 1992 or the second half of 1992 or throughout the whole of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Almost throughout the whole of 1992. I'm not sure, but I think that the red van was operating throughout 1992. A white Mercedes, a blue -- I think it was a Volkswagen; they were there at the beginning, I think, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've completed my questions, Your Honour. Thank you. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Thank you. That's the end of it. We have finished with you. I wish on behalf of the Chamber to thank you for having accepted to come over and to give evidence before this Tribunal. And you will now be escorted out by the usher and be taken care of and returned to where you would like to go. We are also making sure that in going out of this courtroom, you will not be seen by any of the members of the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And I wish you success in your future work, and I hope you will successfully complete the task you have undertaken. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May my legal assistant be excused for a couple of minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. And let's wait, because I think now we go in -- we stay in public session, and I don't want the curtains down, or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But, Your Honour, I think we'll have to go in private session to discuss the matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. I think we need first to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll wait a little bit until the usher returns, and we'll lift the curtains. In the meantime, I think we're going to change the tapes now. So that will require about three minutes before we start. Yes. We need to -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you like to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think Ms. Korner would like --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in case, because I'm going to deal with the Rule 70 motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to deal with the motions or with just the motion from Mr. Ackerman to delay the production of witnesses 7.223 and 224?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to deal with that motion but also with Madam Fauveau's motion, because it doesn't seem to me that requires --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that -- I don't think it -- we need to be in private session for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the discussion about the witnesses and Mr. Ackerman's motion to delay, I'm just anxious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No. I will put your mind at rest, and we'll go into private session. That's the safest way to proceed, even though I tend to disagree with you. I mean, I have read and reread his motion under --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I should add, I don't think -- I've dealt with what I want to say about the witness, so we can stay out of private session for the remainder of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner. So number one was Tuesday next we will be sitting as usual. And the next thing is you are aware that the Prosecutor has informed -- come forward with the information with regard to Rule 92 bis statements for the Sanski Most municipality, so much so that there has already been a formal objection forthcoming from the bench for the Defence team for General Talic. We have heard nothing from you, Mr. Ackerman. So more or less I would imagine there's -- time is still running in your favour. But more or less we wanted to know, since the Sanski Most municipality is approaching, whether to expect anything from you or whether the situation is, as it obtains now, and we can deal with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I -- my position with regard to that is I met with Madam Fauveau, and we went through these together, and she --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She filed an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She indicated she would file an objection to basically all of them, I think. And so I decided it didn't make any sense for me to just copy and that file that. So that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, I think we may need to go back in private session as a result of what we were discussing before the break. But before we do that, can I say this: That in respect of the Rule 92 aspect -- I know that Your Honour mentioned that you are -- I'm not sure I was here. But I heard it anyhow -- were disinclined to issue guidelines. I understand that, Your Honour, but I think it may be important particularly in relation to the aspect that really concerns Madam Fauveau, which is that each of these witnesses does say in some form or another that the offences which, as I understand it, they don't dispute the fact of the offences or the crimes. It's whether Serb soldiers were involved. And this is a problem, Your Honour, that I think we will need guidance on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, definitely. I didn't say that the Chamber is disinclined generally speaking, or as a rule. It's a question of will it restrict itself to what it considers to be necessary. And as we go along --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Don't expect a set of guidelines which then possibly could be used either by the Prosecution or by the Defence, not these teams but other -- by other teams in other cases and -- with the consequence that I have to sit with other Judges and explain this and explain that. So it's more or less -- you know, I mean, when we hand down guidelines, they tend to be taken as guidelines of the Tribunal, while they may well be guidelines of the particular Trial Chamber as composed for a particular case. So more or less, do expect some guidelines but not as -- or along the lines that sort of you gave us the impression -- when I say "you," the three of you -- gave us the impression that you were expecting. I mean, there will be some guidelines, but as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think I know what Your Honour was referring to in light of my discussions with Judge Schomburg the other day. Your Honour, can I ask, then, to go back into private session just to deal with the matter that Madam Fauveau raised, because I think it's quite important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything further? Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The second matter on the motion on behalf of General Talic is the third paragraph from the end, which I think I ought to correct, which we suggest is a misstatement of fact. It says: "The Prosecution has been granted excessive power in being able to choose which entities can come under the provisions of Rule 70, since the Rule includes no definition of the fortunate beneficiaries of these exceptional arrangement. And it is even forbidden to name them in public." We don't choose anything. Organisations and individuals supply documents within -- even if they don't use the word "Rule 70," under the conditions which apply to Rule 70. It's not that the Prosecution pick and choose anything. Your Honour, otherwise, I don't think there's anything further that I want to say about the motion. It clearly supports Mr. Ackerman, and we have responded in full to that. The only matter that I really want to stress is this: It is our submission that all of this is an attempt to prevent Your Honours from hearing what is clearly cogent and relevant evidence from independent persons, one of the few independent persons, present during this conflict. And we suggest that it is important for the ascertainment of the truth of these events that Your Honours hear this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, just to direct to your attention to what this Trial Chamber considers to be relevant and important. Number one: Let's keep separate and distinct your latest or most recent motion; namely, the one filed on the 15th of April yesterday or the day before yesterday to delay the testimony of the two scheduled witnesses, 7.223 and 7.224, and the previous motion, which to this Trial Chamber is the more important of the two, namely the motion challenging -- challenging the legality of Rule 70. There is, of course, the previous motion for an order -- order but let's not discuss that for the time being and concentrate on these two only. What I would like to hear from you is the following: There are two possibilities. Possibility number one is that well before the first of these two witnesses is due in The Hague, we would have handed down our decision on your motion dealing with the alleged illegality of Rule 70. That is one possibility. And we are working on that possibility first. We are trying first and foremost to put our priorities right and try and decide that matter first and foremost. Now, what would be the position with regard to your motion to delay the testimony of these two scheduled witnesses in that eventuality? That's number one. Number two: If we encounter difficulties which can be of various kinds, which would make it impossible for -- to us -- for us to hand down our decision on Rule 70, pending the handing down of that decision what should be our decision with regard to your motion for the -- for delaying the production of these two witnesses. Now, you put two forward -- two main reasons in your motion. And that's in paragraph 6 of your motion of two days ago. And I would like you to address those two reasons in the light of what I have just told you and also in the light of the objections or response of -- oral response of Ms. Korner earlier on in today's sitting. And stick to that. I mean, avoid getting -- going into the merits of your motion dealing with Rule 70, except and insofar as it may -- it may in one or more events possibly lead us to the conclusion that we should put an obstacle to the coming forward of these two witnesses. And then there is one last thing that Ms. Korner did not mention and that I wouldn't expect you to mention but I would remind you of: That this is not a court of justice sitting with a lay jury where sometimes mistakes are made which -- to which there is no remedy except quashing. In other words, where mistakes are remediably committed sometimes. This is a Trial Chamber with professional Judges who have absolutely no difficult at all if needs be to go backwards in time and cancel a part of a disposition or the totality of the disposition. May I also remind you of what was decided in Blaskic, precisely with regard to Rule 70, leaving doors open in certain eventualities when the Trial Chamber at any given moment would sense the danger of prejudicing the right to a fair trial of the accused, reserving the right precisely to do what I have just mentioned or to stop an evidence where it is and sort of remove it from its agenda. So with that on your desk, Mr. Ackerman, you may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want to, first of all, tell you that I object very strongly to the Prosecutor's remark that what I'm trying to do here is prevent witnesses from coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would tend to agree with you. The Trial Chamber at no time has looked upon or tends to look or even just suspects that that could be your intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I think my client's rights are being violated under the Statute of this Tribunal, it's not -- it's not just something I should do, but it's my duty, my obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I bring that to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we have told you -- we have told you before as a Trial Chamber that we've taken your objection to Rule 70 very seriously, and it's going to be one of the motions that -- on which we are going to hand down comprehensive written decision, not just an oral decision but a comprehensive written decision, because we think it touches upon something which is fundamental in any criminal process, and that is the right to a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
