utterances.text: The other thing, Your Honour, is I think there is an unfortunate mixing of issues here that has complicated today beyond where it needed to be. The motion that I filed yesterday does not relate to my motion with regard to Rule 70 at all. The only relationship between the two is this happens to deal with evidence that was acquired by the Prosecutor pursuant to Rule 70. But beyond that, it doesn't affect it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me stop you awhile, Mr. Ackerman. This is why I told you to refer to para 6 of your most recent motion. And although para 6, second paragraph number 13 refers to the motion of the 6th of March, in reality what it says is that it is your contention that there is something basically wrong which could lead to a -- an egregious violation of an equality of arms -- of the equality of arms principle. And the only place where you have questioned the equality of arms substantially is in your motion attacking, challenging, the legality of Rule 70, not in your first motion. In your first motion, you said they have given information to the Prosecution; they haven't given information to us; they haven't even answered our letter. This is not equality of arms. But what you're saying here is basically something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To the first one, there could still be a remedy. To the second one, the question remains open. So let's say that there is a little bit of confusion of the two issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But basically the way the Chamber is reading this second paragraph, which we have highlighted here in particular of para 6, is precisely because it is very intimately related to your motion dealing with the totality of Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The position that I'm taking with regard to this motion, Your Honour, is this: The first thing that you must consider is that we are dealing with an organisation -- are we in a private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We are not in private session. We are in public session. But you don't need to mention the organisation. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We do need to go to private session for just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to private session for just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other thing that needs to be part of your consideration is this: We are also dealing with an organisation that has, based upon rulings of this Tribunal, the right to assert immunity. Now, the question that I think implicates Article 21 of the Statute, the equality of arms principle, the rights of the accused is this: Can an organisation, especially one of the nature of this one, take the position that we will provide documents and information to the Prosecutor of the Tribunal that the Prosecutor believes will be helpful in convicting the people who they have on trial? But we will assert our right to immunity with regard to documents in our possession that might be helpful to a defendant who is an accused in this Tribunal. I think the answer to that is no. I think that can't happen. That violates, Your Honour, just almost word for word Article 21(4)(e), giving the defendant the right "to examine, or have examined, the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as the witnesses against him." This is not a matter probably over which any of us in this room have a great deal of control. If that organisation wants to assert its immunity rights with regard to requests that I make of them, bona fide requests that I make of them, I'm not sure that even the Tribunal can prevent them from doing that. But it certainly creates an unbelievably unfair situation. This issue has nothing to do -- or it's peripheral to the issue of cross-examination of these witnesses that are set out in the motion that I filed yesterday. It might be -- it may very well be that if I am given the same kind of document access, the same quality of document access that the Prosecution was given, that I will find documents that will be helpful in the cross-examination of these witnesses. But more than that, I have a right under 21(4)(e) to bring witnesses from that organisation and have them bring documents with them that I think are relevant to my client's defence and sit here in this witness stand the same way the Prosecution wants to have a witness do and identify those documents and put them before Your Honours, or to bring a witness who was in the area at the time and knows things about what happened in the area that are helpful to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that -- if you are correct in this assertion or in what you are contending, Mr. Ackerman, on what grounds would you base your suggestion that you are in a disadvantaged position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm in a disadvantaged position if this organisation decides that it's going to cooperate with the Prosecution and not with the Defence. It's an enormously disadvantageous position. We will give -- we will give the Prosecution documents to help convict, but we don't give the Defence documents to help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I suggested to you to keep separate and distinct the two issues altogether, because in reality if we start discussing Rule 70, we will not be discussing whether there should be a delay of the production of these two witnesses, but we would be discussing whether there is any violation of Article 21, in particular Article 21 para 4 of the Statute. That's not the point. The whole point is this: Even assuming for the time being, just for the grace of the argument, for argument's sake, that you may be right in part in your submissions regarding the legality of Rule 70, do you see a valid reason why these two witnesses ought not to be brought forward as scheduled considering two things: Number one that the only instance where you are not put at par with the Prosecution in Rule 70 is where you are requested, should you elect to take advantage of Rule 70 itself as an accused, as a defendant, to first seek the approval, the authorisation of this Tribunal. That's -- while the Prosecution is not. The Prosecution may avail itself of Rule 70 without the Tribunal even knowing, being aware of that, while you are not in the same position. If that is so, how would it necessarily or how should or ought it necessarily bring this Trial Chamber to the conclusion to stay the production of these two witnesses, considering also a further point: That the right of the Prosecution and also your right, given the authorisation of the Court not to disclose the material to the other party, refers only to that information which is tendered to the Prosecution or to you on a confidential basis and -- this is where the Trial Chamber lays its emphasis -- which has been - has been - in the past used solely for the purpose of generating new evidence. The moment either the Prosecution or the moment you, as Defence counsel, decide to make that one further step forward and use that information by tendering it in evidence, no longer are you covered -- can you claim to be covered by the right not to disclose. And this is of fundamental importance. This is not -- no longer a case where you can claim that the Prosecution has a right to hide from you the evidence or the statement of these two persons it intends to bring forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've never claimed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are asking for the delay in the production of these two persons. Now, you may have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- valid arguments to bring forward that you require time to prepare for your cross-examination, but that again should be something -- something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, this is not a Rule 70 motion. It's not a Rule 70 argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I told you -- this is why I told you keep them separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I don't make an argument that there's no Rule 70 implication with regard to this matter. My argument is much simpler than that. It is that it is incredibly unfair for this organisation to say, "We will cooperate with one side. We will give the Tribunal evidence that helps convict, but we will not cooperate with the other side and give evidence that may acquit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's the point. Now, just let me finish. Because that's the position that we're in right now. Now, negotiations are going on, and it may very well be that those negotiations will result in us having the same kind of document access that the Prosecutor has. They may very well wind up that way. But they -- they could also take the position that we're going to assert our immunity and not let you see any documents or give you any documents. If they do that, I can't imagine how it's anything but just horribly unfair for you to allow the Prosecutor to use evidence they got from that organisation that helps -- that arguably helps convict people in this Tribunal and not -- not see that there's a huge violation of the defendant's rights under Article 21(4)(e): The Prosecution can bring witnesses from that organisation and I can't. And how on earth does that comport with a statutory provision that says I can summon witnesses under the same conditions as they can? I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But you yourself stated that you have that right. This is why I asked you before if you assert -- if you seriously believe that you have the right to summon witnesses from that organisation, bring them forward, put questions to them, ask them to confirm or deny the authenticity of documents, ask them to bring over documents belonging or not belonging to that organisation. If you seriously believe and assert that you have that right -- and I'm not telling you that you don't have that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have the right to ask for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But where is the disadvantaged position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I have the right to ask for that. But they have the right to say, "No, we are going to assert immunity with regard to you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You wait. As the Trial Chamber once said in Blaskic -- you wait until that happens and then you visit the problem then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It happened already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it hasn't happened. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now we're in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have had two instances, one from General Talic. And at that point in time, we had to tell General Talic, "You haven't even asked the humanitarian organisation to provide you with the documents."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But exactly. At the same time, this was happening, you filed your motion and the basis for your request was precisely that you had written to the humanitarian organisation, and this humanitarian organisation had not written back to you. That was the position in time when you filed your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When we came to discuss it here, they had just answered you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- In a way as to open doors but not necessarily conclude the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the situation is status quanti. I mean, it's as it was a month ago. It hasn't changed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No it hasn't changed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes it has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're still waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. I got a letter back from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When? Because the last information you gave us --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So the information is that they have written to you, asking for information from you, as we gathered, and that negotiations are still underway --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I heard from them a week ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But listen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I've now written back to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you yourself -- you are maintaining that the situation is still open, and you yourself are hopeful that the door is not closed, making it impossible for you to obtain all the information that you have asked for from this humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I may be being way too literal about this, Your Honour, but I have asked them for permission to show you the latest letter that they sent me, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. You told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They said in there that I should share it with no one. And I'm taking them literal. I'm quite certain that they didn't mean that I shouldn't share it with the Court. But until they tell me that, I think I should err on the side of caution. But it would shed light on what we're doing right now if I could show you that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I think this Trial Chamber has made it very clear from the very, very outset of this trial that we never doubt a single word of what you state in this courtroom. So what you say is taken as -- as the situation, but it doesn't change anything. All the options are open, including a negative response -- a final negative response from the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So but the whole -- the whole issue, I mean, should be debated when it arises, not hypothetically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Until they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why should we go into the question and decide how we should deal with this humanitarian organisation, or with some witnesses, or information provided by this humanitarian organisation, not knowing what this humanitarian organisation is going to tell you or how it's going to be dealing with your request? Maybe it's the way your request is being put that isn't digested well by the humanitarian organisation, or maybe they will say, "Yes, you are right. We will treat you exactly the same as we are treating the Prosecution." When we went in private session for that few seconds, I think you also ought to give proper weight to the significance of what you said at that point in time, who this organisation is and if it's part of whatever you said, does it make more sense the way you put it or the way it has acted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's a matter of just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- no, I would like you to think about it, because you are in exactly the same position. You may have, for example, let's say another organisation. You may have, for example, the government of -- a foreign government or you may have the secret service of a foreign government or you may have at your disposal archives of a foreign government which are not at the disposal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But I said you may, or you might.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Theoretically, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes theoretically. I mean, put yourself, then, in the that position, hypothetically, and try to argue along the lines that I have been arguing. So let's say there is a foreign government that is all out committed to help your client, for example. So there is a vested interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I understand your point, Your Honour. I don't think it changes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This Tribunal exists for what it stands for in terms of its Statute. It has been created by the United Nations because it is an ad hoc Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it has a mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour Article 21(4) does not set out the rights of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It sets out the rights of the accused. And I'm talking about the rights of the accused. And it doesn't say in here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Those are the rights that will be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't say in here that the Prosecutor has the right to acquire witnesses under the same conditions that I do. Now they do but it doesn't say that. I'm not talking about that. I'm talking about the defendant's right to have witnesses under the same conditions as the Prosecutor. And if the conditions the Prosecutor has is an organisation that says, "We'll cooperate with you," and my conditions are an organisation that says, "We won't cooperate with you." It's the same organisation. That's unfair, that violates 21(4). That's my argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's hypothetical. It could violate -- given certain circumstances, maybe the Tribunal will come to that conclusion. But not necessarily. It depends. This is why reading the decision in Blaskic, it is very important, because there you have a hint -- a clear hint at what the rationale of Rule 70 is or looks like it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the concern of that Trial Chamber all along was given that something like Rule 70 is important within the context of such a Tribunal, our concern is how to make sure that the due process and fair trial rights of the accused are protected throughout the Trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think it's very simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it is -- exactly. Your contention is a radical one. I mean, if this organisation cooperates with the Prosecution but is not prepared to cooperate with us, then the solution is a radical one: No witnesses from that humanitarian organisation. Well, I'm not telling you here and now that that is or should be infallibly and always the -- the only necessary consequence. It could be. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing radical about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Unless you think Article 21(4)(e) is radical. There's nothing radical about my taking the position that I should have the same access to material that they have. That's not radical. That's -- that's the law. That's not radical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you are exactly in the same position. If you were given authority -- authorisation by the Trial Chamber with regard to information that you acquire in a confidential matter -- manner and which you have used solely in generating evidence, you are exactly in the same position as the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you think I'm in the same position, go ahead and issue the subpoena and watch how fast they assert immunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sure they will assert immunity. But also the fact remains that they haven't told you no as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's why we need to wait. Why open the door and let the horse out before we have to? You have an opportunity to do justice. Why pass up that opportunity? There is no major hurry for those witnesses to come here, no major hurry at all. Now, I understand it's a difficult matter of scheduling, but we're going to be here a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the thing that worries this Tribunal least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It should, it should. Why assume that they're going to cooperate with me the same way they did with the Prosecutor and let this evidence come in and then later find out that they won't and say, "Okay. We're going to ignore what all these people said." That's difficult to do. We're human beings. And we come years from now to a place, and we know we heard things, we're not sure we know where we heard them. And so it's very hard, very difficult. Why put yourselves in that position? Why put yourselves in a position where you might have to do that? Just do justice right up front. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say two things in response, although I'd like to be -- at least start the next witness today if possible. The first is this: Mr. Ackerman repeats endlessly, like a mantra, "The organisation provides evidence to help the Prosecution convict." It does no such thing. It provides the Office of the Prosecutor with the documents that partially Your Honour and the Defence have seen for the purposes of pursuing investigations which we're required to do under the Statute in to what occurred in the territories of Bosnia -- the former Yugoslavia during the conflict. The difficulty, I think, that Mr. Ackerman faces and because of the fact that he's negotiating with the organisation is that if I understand him correctly, he's saying if the Prosecution have been supplied with documents by this organisation, then we must be supplied with any of the documents they've got. And no organisation is going to agree to that. If Mr. Ackerman's concerns are that he wishes the organisation to provide him with material which may be Rule 68, in the terms that it is exculpatory or challenges the credibility of the witnesses we wish to call, then I'm sure that what he ought to be doing is specifying. And that, I think, is probably the difficulty; that he's not. And neither he nor -- I'm sorry. I don't know what it is. But I am concerned that it should not be suggested that organisations are supplying material deliberately aimed at helping the Prosecution to convict. They are supplying material relevant to the period for which they are in possession to enable investigation to be carried out. So Your Honour, I think that ought to be made absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, Ms. Korner either doesn't know or shouldn't know anything about what my request says. But I can tell you that it is quite specific, very specific. The other thing I want to mention is that Ms. Korner raised today is this whole issue of Rule 68. It keeps getting brought up. But we don't tell her what our defence is, and therefore she can't provide Rule 68 material. I have said over and over, and I will say it again because of the record. Our defence is that the Prosecution has an obligation to prove the guilt of my client beyond a reasonable doubt. And I challenge by a plea of not guilty every word of the Prosecutor's indictment. What is Rule 68 material? It is material that tends to show that what the Prosecution alleges in their indictment is not the case. Also it's material that would question the credibility of any witness that the Prosecution calls in this case. Now, that's not a difficult thing for the Prosecution to figure out. And the Prosecution cannot be absolved of their responsibilities under Rule 68 because I am asserting the classic defence in a criminal case, that is, we didn't do this stuff; you prove it. Their obligations under Rule 68 are to provide material that is inconsistent with what they allege in their indictment and material that goes toward the credibility of witnesses they call in this case. That's what it is. It's not hard to understand. And that's what I ask that they provide and I demand that they provide.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that is precisely the problem. Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman says, "We dispute every word of the indictment." In fact, they don't. We've seen that. They say, "We admit to this, or we're prepared to admit if General Talic admits, but we don't want to reveal it." This killing occurred. Your Honour, it is simply not good enough to say, "That's all we're prepared to say. Prove your case," because of course, we do the very best we can to ensure that anything that appears to us on that basis -- in other words, that challenges the credibility, or is inconsistent with what the witness said, is disclosed. But there may be other issues about what simply we don't know. And it's not assistance that we require. And the mantra, the Prosecution has to prove its case doesn't absolve the Defence of its duty. Mr. Ackerman's duty to his client to provide us with what we need to do the relevant searches. And to make a complaint at the end of the day when something comes up, we then appreciate that it's part of the Defence case, which we were unable to appreciate before and we see that there is material that goes to that, well, you should have known that in advance. But Your Honour, I think we've drifted right off the point now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But I want to make it absolutely clear -- that's fine. Mr. Ackerman can maintain this position. And in the event his client is convicted, he can maintain this position before the Appeals Chamber. But it is our contention that this is not a one -- a total one-way street, as Mr. Ackerman contends. He is well aware, as the whole world is, of the huge amount of information that has been supplied to the Office of the Prosecutor, not necessarily obtained through seizures or search warrants but by organisations and individuals. And if there's a real refusal to give any sort of further information, which in fact was required under the Statute, well, then he has only himself to blame if in fact somewhere in the -- buried in the vaults of this institution was a document which had he given us more information might have proved to be of value. So I want to make that absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's my understanding from testimony given by Mr. Inayat right here in this Court that every document that comes into the Prosecutor's office is scanned into the system that you saw in operation here in the courtroom. You can search it in about, I don't know, seconds for any word you want to search for. So it's not like somebody has to go into a room full of documents and paw through them. And I know they've been doing searches looking for these matters. Now, just because I have said that I'm willing to concede that all the killings listed in the indictment occurred does not absolve Ms. Korner of the responsibility of telling all of us if they have evidence that one of those killings didn't occur. So it doesn't -- it doesn't do anything. She still has the obligation to at least be honest with this Tribunal and say, you know, even as Mr. Ackerman concedes that it occurred, we have evidence that it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, let's -- let's redirect our arguments and bring them to an end, to the real issue here. I think -- do you agree with me? We have heard enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We think that we have heard enough submissions on this matter, and we will decide it in good time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. De Roux is on his feet, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, but Maitre de Roux, I -- in your absence these last few days, I complained that I'm going to have a stiff neck having to look at the Defence team of General Talic, because I have to turn my head 45 degrees. Yes. And give my back to Judge Taya, which I don't like to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will be extremely brief regarding this matter. But I think that there are two quite different problems here. There's the problem of substance, and that is the implementation of Rule 70, and that is the requirement by an organisation for protection which is provided by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and its refusal to cooperate with the Defence. And without speaking about this organisation, the secret aspect of it is important. Then there is the problem of knowing whether we can examine the witnesses from that organisation before the Trial Chamber has terminated the debate. Regarding this second point, the Defence of General Talic fully relies on the wisdom of the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber may decide to hear those witnesses before having made a ruling on the motion. It may choose out of prudence to first make a ruling and then hear the witnesses. But in any event, let us make things quite clear. The Defence will perform fully its duty when the witnesses are called, and we will see at that point in time how the witnesses will react. What we would not like is to have this organisation respond -- because we too have contacted them -- we would not like that organisation to say, "The Defence -- we cannot be so precise and take certain side steps, while at the same time clearly and without risking contradiction -- and I repeat that -- without risking the possibility of being contradicted, its support for the Prosecution. But I am saying that we will take that risk of contradicting them. And I think that if an organisation -- if an entity cooperates with the Prosecution, it is quite normal for the Defence at that point in time to have all its rights, notwithstanding the limitations implied by Rule 70, but by applying the provisions of Article 24 [As interpreted] of the Statute. That is all that I intended to say on behalf of the Defence of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Maitre de Roux. To the Chamber, the position is very clear, frankly. I don't think we ought to repeat anything on what -- what we have already stated. Any way, Ms. Korner, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only thing that I would ask then, Your Honour, is that simply if Your Honour is going to -- for Your Honour to make a ruling on Mr. Ackerman's application to delay as soon as possible, because we clearly need to tell the witnesses what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The transcript says that Mr. De Roux mentioned the provisions of Article 24 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 21(4), it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think he meant 21(4). It should say 21(4).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So the discussion on this motion is concluded, and the intention of the Trial Chamber is to hand down its decisions on both matters either simultaneously, and if not simultaneously we'll see which ought to be decided first. But I don't know exactly here and now what we will decide. So we'll take our time. But we will decide in good time, Ms. Korner, not to put you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. It's -- it's really the one that's due at the end of May. He has to be told the position, because he's set aside five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not our intention to delay until the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're just in the middle of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know that, Your Honour. And I know it sounds awful in the sense and -- it's not what -- he really -- he is somebody who has a full diary and has set aside five days for the purposes of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the position is very simple. Actually, with regard to point -- Rule 70, there's, I think, just one big issue to be decided. The rest is not that important. But we still have to -- to see to that. And with regard to this present motion, there isn't much to say, keeping in mind particularly what has been said in Blaskic, because Blaskic in its simplicity went deep and to the heart of the matter, and that is definitely not the intention of -- at least at present -- of this Tribunal to depart much from what was decided in that case. So that closes the matter for the time being. I -- if I remember well, the next witness is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is in closed session. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have to bring down the curtains. We'll go into closed session immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask you -- is Your Honour sitting till half past 6.00 or 7.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Till half past 6.00. At least to see his or her face.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I say, I can do a few background preliminaries and leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also to tell you frankly, I mean, we were only handed the statement this morning or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why that is, Your Honour, because it was handed in quite sometime ago. So it's -- this, I can say, has got nothing to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: at 6.32 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of April, 2002, at 2.15p.m.
